title: The Penny Jar That Pays for Coffee
body: There's a small ceramic jar on my kitchen counter. It's nothing special, just something that came with a set of mugs years ago. For months, it sat empty, a silent monument to good intentions. Then one day, I decided to actually use it for its intended purpose. Holding the change from my pockets at the end of each day. The first few weeks were unremarkable. A quarter here, a dime there. It felt like a game of how little I could contribute. But then something interesting happened. The jar started to fill up. Not quickly, but steadily. It became a quiet, physical manifestation of a small, consistent action. I'm not going to tell you this jar made me rich. That's not how compounding works, especially with pocket change. What it did do was teach me something no finance course ever could. The power of the boring win. Every day, without fail, I'd empty my pockets. The jar became a habit, so automatic I didn't even think about it. It wasn't about deprivation; it was just about noticing the small stuff. The money wasn't working for me in any traditional sense, but it was accumulating in a way that felt real and tangible. Last week, the jar was full. I took it to the grocery store, poured the contents onto the counter, and started counting. It's a surprisingly meditative process, actually. There was $23.47 in there. Enough for a decent bag of coffee beans and a nice loaf of bread. No free lunch, of course. That money came from me, piece by piece. But seeing it all laid out, the sum of countless tiny decisions, was more rewarding than any stock market chart I've ever seen. The tag tells the truth. The little things add up. Now the jar is empty again, waiting to be filled. The question I'm handing to you is. What's your jar?
